speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Today, I will speak on our patients and our healthcare workers, our healthcare system and our pandemic defence.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our people want to live at home, and sometimes, when a patient has an incurable terminal illness, that patient may want to die at home as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And if the policy intention is to subsidise the care, it is important to look at whether the subsidy and support follow the patient as well, including into the home.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is important in end-of-life care, palliative care.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is important when patients are less mobile because each trip to and fro for a less mobile senior can mean expenses on a taxi trip, a private hired vehicle or even a private ambulance for some of the sickest patients who are based at home.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As family sizes get smaller, with fewer children to share the filial duties of caregiving, accompanying a parent to a clinic, each visit, each trip to and fro, means cutting into family care leave, annual leave from work.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And, sometimes, that leads of friction with the employer.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is often the less well-off workers, with less bargaining power, who face difficulty being a caregiver because we know that while some employers are kind, some employers are "one kind".

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Last year, during the debate on Healthier SG, I shared about one of our Clementi seniors.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The Minister also said, "This will naturally have to be reviewed as we shift our paradigm".

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Care is moving "beyond hospital to community", the Ministry of Health's (MOH's) own words from half a decade ago.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The Healthcare Services Act (HCSA) recognises that healthcare goes beyond places of brick-and-mortar.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The National Electronic Health Record (NEHR) also recognises that patients move between different places of care and so, there has to be continuity of medical records as part of the continuity of care.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is a natural policy progression to look at how subsidies can be made more portable with the appropriate processes and safeguards, so that care follows the patient, including to the home for patients who are less mobile.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Traditionally, MediSave was tied to the inpatient hospital setting.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But over the years, we now allow MediSave to be used for outpatient care of chronic diseases in the clinic.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But more can be done because some patients at home have medical conditions and it is very hard for them to move around, very hard to go out of the home, to a clinic.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For instance, patients with chronic neurological conditions, such as muscular dystrophy or motor neuron disease.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some patients may be homebound because of old age.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And so each trip going out, not so straightforward.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And there are also some patients, some seniors, with incurable illnesses, terminal illnesses, with limited time left.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And for these patients, every trip to and from a healthcare facility means less time spent at home, less time at home with loved ones in a place that they want to be.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can MOH look at how healthcare financing and healthcare delivery can be made more portable for such patients?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So that care can be delivered at home, closer to home, especially if the intent is already to subsidise such care.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When patients need to do a blood test a few days before the appointment, can MOH make it more straightforward for patients to have these blood tests done at home, or at a polyclinic near to home, to reduce the distance travelled by patients and caregivers?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can MOH make blood test forms more portable across the different public healthcare institutions?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: My Clementi residents tell me of fellow Singaporeans being discharged from one public hospital, being given blood test forms to be brought to their regular doctor at another public hospital and that the doctor at the second public hospital, their regular doctor, has to reorder, reprint, reissue the blood test form, even though both hospitals were part of the same healthcare cluster.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There is more that can be done to make the journey smoother for our patients.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In short, policy design must be about seeing through the eyes of our people, because that is how we make better policies and deliver better care.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I want to move on to talk about our healthcare workers and in particular, Flexible Work Arrangements (FWAs) in healthcare.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Amidst our ageing population in Singapore, many healthcare workers are caregivers themselves as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There is the filial son, the filial daughter, who works a full shift at work in the hospital, comes home, put in that extra mile for their parents too, that extra mile at work, the extra mile as the caregiver after knocking off work, looking after an aged parent who may have dementia, or themselves have a serious illness.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There are single mothers working in healthcare on the healthcare frontlines.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When they finish their shift, they go home and look after their children, putting their full hearts in at work and at home.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There are also healthcare workers who themselves have special needs children at home.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Each time a healthcare worker faces challenges with FWAs, it poses challenges at home as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some healthcare workers have themselves fallen ill with a serious illness, such as cancer.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They have gone through treatment, fighting their way back to health, rebuilding their health even as they rebuild their work identity, trying to make progress, trying to come back to work and helping patients who are recovering from their illnesses.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, FWAs can make the difference between healthcare workers having to choose between their family and their job, or – in some cases – between their health and their job.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I also want to speak for our older healthcare workers.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: These healthcare workers have served on the frontline for decades, full of experience and wisdom.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But, sometimes, they also are looking for FWAs as they have elderly parents at home.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We should find ways to keep these workers in the workforce serving, as long as they are able to and wish to do so.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Progressive, supportive Human Resources practices, it matters in the workplace; it matters in healthcare.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It keeps the workplace open to sisters and brothers coming from different backgrounds, different walks of life, different personal journeys.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It helps us recruit and retain the full diversity and depth of talent and life experience that is Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And all this adds to the team because healthcare is, fundamentally, a human endeavour, no matter how much technology and science there is.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Healthcare is fundamentally about human endeavour and humanity.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And when our workforce draws on a full breadth of experience, life experience, talent, diversity, it helps our healthcare system.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I want to speak on our system of healthcare.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Mr Lim Siong Guan was the former Head of Civil Service.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I remember a quote which the Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat mentioned in a speech at an MOH event in 2017, "Implementation is policy", that is what Mr Lim Siong Guan said. "Implementation is policy", because the effectiveness of policy is not measured by how elegant it looks on paper, but how it is translated into reality during implementation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, I want to ask MOH some questions on implementation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When can our residents start joining Healthier SG?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What about patients with chronic diseases, who are already seeing an established doctor in the community?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: How will the subsidy and financing frameworks operate for chronic disease medications?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And how will it interlock with the existing model of care that many family doctors provide?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And how will this connect with wellness and exercise programmes in the community?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because my residents in Clementi and in Faber Hills within Clementi, tell me that the Health Promotion Board (HPB) was, at one point, cutting back on exercise programmes in the community.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And this meant that some seniors had to travel further, in order to access their usual exercise programmes of their choice.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On IT, or information technology, with Healthier SG, many more general practitioners (GPs) and family doctor clinics will join our national healthcare IT systems.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We owe it to patients and healthcare workers to ensure these IT systems are best-in-class, not just best in Singapore, but best in the world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On New Year's Eve last year, the New York Times had a sharply written article on IT and software design and maintenance.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The author talked about "technical debt". "Technical debt" is the gap between what software is and what we want it to be.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This "technical debt" is paid not by the software developers or manufacturers. "Technical debt" is paid by users.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In healthcare IT, "technical debt" is paid by patients and healthcare workers – waiting for computers to load, windows to open.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: How many mouse clicks and how many keystrokes does it take to make something happen?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And with more private clinics plugging into the national IT system for healthcare, there will be far more than 14 million consults a year, depending on that infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, it is all the more important we ensure our IT infrastructure in healthcare is best-in-class, not just in Singapore, but internationally around the world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Last year, I asked if this is something GovTech can look at?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The Minister-in-charge of GovTech also sits in MOH.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Is there an opportunity for deeper synergy, a healthcare IT platform built by Singaporeans for Singaporeans, good enough to compete against the best in the world?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is a matter of funding, willpower, ambition and vision.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I want to talk about why time is care.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The 1993 White Paper on Affordable Healthcare mentioned this.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But there can also be other kinds of market failure.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I spoke up on this 10 years ago, in an article in The Straits Times.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If a clinic is too busy and consultation times are too short, it becomes harder to promote health.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And in our ageing society, with patients having more medical conditions, our healthcare system must allow sufficient time because time is as much a part of healthcare, as clinics and hospitals, medication and technology.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Time with someone you have just met to build trust and rapport for a long journey down the road.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Time with a young Singaporean facing a mental wellness challenge.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Time with someone who has just been diagnosed with a life-changing situation, and you are talking to that person, connecting, understanding their hopes and fears, preparing for the journey ahead.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And so, whether it is our family doctors' clinics' operations, healthcare IT or the real-world journey of patients and families, our policymakers must continue seeing through the eyes of the people to understand what happens in real life, on the ground.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Otherwise, even the brightest policymaker is flying an aircraft through a storm without instruments, not knowing the airspeed, altitude or how much is in the fuel tank.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On our pandemic defence, we need to learn the right lessons of a generation, from the crisis of a generation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Excess deaths – I asked this in Parliament.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What was the impact of people delaying care and screening due to pandemic fear?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Did socioeconomic status and housing affect COVID-19 outcomes and excess deaths?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On securing our supplies in a challenging world, is MOH working with the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) to strengthen our supply chains?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If there needs to be a new vaccine, can Singapore innovate and manufacture it on shore?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I asked this in the Budget debate two years ago.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for Health serves in both MOH and MinLaw, and I hope the agencies will study this too.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I said this three years ago during the debate on the President's Address.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Healthcare is about our people's lives – your life and mine, the lives of our loved ones, the life of every Singaporean.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Last year, I spoke up to MOH about change – A Change Agenda.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And as we emerge from the pandemic, it is a time for choosing.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: A time for choosing how we shape the future ahead.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Longevity science offers great potential for boosting the healthspan of Singaporeans, particularly seniors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The People's Action Party (PAP) senior group believes that this will be a gamechanger.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Indeed, researchers have made remarkable strides in understanding the ageing process.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Studies have shown that various preventive measures can extend our healthspan, which is the amount of time we spend in good health.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It is now possible to stay healthier than one's age – or what scientists term as "chronological age" – would imply with the correct lifestyle and medical intervention.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Furthermore, biomarker tests can now be used to measure a person's biological age more accurately, allowing us to better monitor our healthspan.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Lifestyle changes like intermittent fasting and exercises are already known to be beneficial.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: There is also the possibility of clinical interventions, such as new supplements, existing drugs adapted for healthy longevity and novel drugs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: To accomplish this, much work needs to be done to turn cutting-edge research into clinical and lifestyle interventions in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It will also take time to convince and train local healthcare practitioners to adopt longevity science.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And could MOH tell us how we can equip our healthcare professionals with the knowledge for this growing field of healthcare?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This year, we will see the launch of Healthier SG, which will transform the way healthcare is delivered.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Our people will be empowered to take care of their quality of life through preventive and dedicated patient-doctors relation.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This is a paradigm shift from reactively caring for those who are already sick to proactively preventing healthy individuals from falling ill.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This big shift in our approach for healthcare is for everyone.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: As our population ages, if we do not change our current healthcare model, our healthcare expenditure will be increasing exponentially.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, a change of mindset and the healthcare model is now currently required, to make sure that quality healthcare remains affordable in the future.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We have talked a lot about the ageing population and I think my colleague Ms Poh Li San has mentioned about the "grey rhino", which is a highly probable, high impact, yet neglected trap that will happen.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: With ageing demographics, we will see an increased prevalence of chronic diseases, such as diabetes, hypertension and hyperlipidemia with its consequential diseases in cardiovascular, such as strokes and heart diseases.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: On the other hand, we have smaller families now, which means there will be greater burden for those who are caring for their seniors, as mentioned by Deputy Prime Minister Wong in his Budget statement.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We are fortunate to have various Government endowment funds, from Elder Care Fund and MediFund, to finance various programmes on an ongoing basis.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: On the other hand, we have Healthier SG now, which will take care of another facet of healthcare, and you address how our citizens can live a good, healthy and meaningful life ahead.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We must give full support for Healthier SG, both towards citizens, as well as the medical profession.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How many family doctors have come on board, and what is MOH doing to engage those who have not signed up by now for the buy-in?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: For Singaporeans above 60 years old who will be the first batch to be signed up, how will this be carried out?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How will they be paired with their family doctors and what if their current family doctors did not sign up for Healthier SG?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Today, we are seeing a rise in cost of living due to high inflation.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Medical expenses are not spared, as premiums for medical insurance have gone up as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Across all sectors of healthcare expenses from rental, utility, salaries and operating costs, the cost of running healthcare institutions have risen over the past three years as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: As our medical facilities are acquiring more advanced medical technologies, the cost of treatment would have risen accordingly.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The Government should look into reining in this infrastructure cost of public healthcare institution as that every available space in a healthcare setting is properly planned for optimal utilisation.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Not every single public hospital lobby need to look like a five-star hotel or a shopping centre.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This can help to tame capital expenses and costs for subsequent maintenance.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What measures are MOH taking to tame medical inflation and what is the Government doing to help Singapore cope with the increasing out-of-pocket medical expenses?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Will MOH review the current withdrawal limits of MediSave and increase it, so as to reduce the out-of-pocket expenses for our citizens?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Healthier SG is a major initiative of MOH.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Would MOH update us on the progress and challenges of getting GPs on board this initiative?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I understand that many GPs make profits from dispensing medicines.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: At the same time, many residents have told me that they look forward to buying chronic diseases medication from GPs at a price that is comparable to the price charged by polyclinics.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: At the community level, we have many activities – such as zumba, qigong, gardening, to name a few – that are very healthy and suitable for the elderly and all ages.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: How would MOH facilitate the linkage between the GPs and the community, so that the GPs in our community can recommend their patients to enrol in such healthy activities?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Meanwhile, many community clubs are organising health carnivals for residents over 50 years old.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Would MOH be keen to tap on such health carnivals to encourage senior citizens to sign up for Healthier SG?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If so, the Nanyang division would be the first one to volunteer.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, I had quite severe childhood asthma when I was growing up, but I have the GPs in my neighbourhood to thank for treating me and enabling me to grow up a healthy woman.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I, thus, applaud the Government's move to place key roles on our primary care doctors in the Healthier SG initiative.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I was hopeful that this substantial annual funding will make it business viable for most GPs, who operate business models and face cost pressures, just like any small- and medium-sized enterprises to fully support Healthier SG.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nonetheless, when I asked the GPs I know, there seems to be some mixed feelings and a need for further clarity around a few matters.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, while there will be a capitated service fee, how much of the GPs' current revenue will be impacted by the new subsidies criteria on the medications?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, what form of IT capabilities will be provided, especially if GPs are to treat more chronic disease patients and how will the set-up and recurrent costs of maintaining such IT capabilities be covered?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Third, with more enrolled patients, there will inevitably be added administrative overheads.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While such are often regarded as deadweight costs in public financing, they are real costs to GPs and how will they be supported?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lastly, before 3 April 2020, the Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) subsidies and MediSave were not permitted for any telehealth or telemedicine services.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: During COVID-19, from 3 April 2020 and subsequently, 9 October 2020, a time-limited exception was provided by MOH for patients to use CHAS and MediSave for their regular follow-ups for all chronic conditions under the CDMP through video consultation.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, I think I am not alone in benefiting from traditional Chinese herbs and medicines.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While most of us would not be able to explain why TCM helps in improving various health conditions, almost all who believe in TCM know intuitively that there must be scientific reasons involved in the many herbs that nature provides and the non-invasive methods that work with our bodies which TCM adopts, to improve our health.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The privilege to work with western medicine-trained doctors with strong research capabilities in the past few years has opened my knowledge on systematic and well-designed clinical research, that helps to provide data and insights for evidence-based conclusions on health intervention efficacy.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: — Review Board of our public health institutions and the standards for healthcare efficacy assessments by MOH.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, I would like to repeat the call that I have made during the debate on Healthier SG for the Ministry to pay attention to removing the particular barriers to health-seeking behaviours facing this segment and ensure that our Healthier SG strategy is inclusive socioeconomically.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We need to pay attention to improving seemingly basic things like nutrition, sleep, smoking cessation and exercise, through targeted interventions for this segment because these things may not be basic for them.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And we need to better bring social service officers and agencies into the framework of healthcare clusters and the primary care network (PCN), so as to tighten the nexus between social service and health for the lower income.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Could the Ministry share more about its plans in this regard?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would be reasonable to conclude that unsuccessful applications were turned down because the injuries were determined not to have been caused by the vaccines.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Considering that there has only been such a short time to understand the side effects of vaccines, I would like to ask the Minister a few questions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What threshold does MOH use to decide that a person is eligible for a payout?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Must the vaccine be proven to have caused the effects suffered before payouts are made, or are payouts made if it cannot be proven that the effects were due to some other cause?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Or are there some other tests or thresholds being used?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When more information becomes available over the years, can the unsuccessful applications be reconsidered?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: They are the backbone of our ageing care system and should be recognised and supported more formally.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I spoke about "Carefare" in Parliament in the past two Committees of Supply (COSes) and I advocate for it a third time now.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Because of how retirement adequacy in Singapore is tied so much to employment, caregivers who give up their most productive earning years because of care needs in their families are exposed to old age poverty, and this cannot be right.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Bringing forward financial support mitigates the stress faced by caregivers over finances, anxiety towards their own ageing, which contributes to long-term chronic health conditions like hypertension and diabetes, among others.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: These will, in turn, exacerbate the healthcare cost burden down the road, which will only get worse as our population ages.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Why do we wait to give, if giving now can help us to save more costs in future?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Other than direct income support, MOH can help redistribute the day-to-day care load from caregivers' shoulders by helping to scale community solutions.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This can also prevent caregivers from having to give up their jobs in the first place.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Nee Soon South is piloting a Caregiver Resource Centre, where a peer support network is being built for caregivers.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: And this initiative helped me to see the potential of the grassroots to be tapped for this purpose.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I urge MOH to partner with the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY) to build the community's ageing care capacity through the People's Association (PA) platform.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We can even explore creating a time-banking system in the likes of Japan's model which allows seniors to swap services for free.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: They provide companionship, help run errands, cook for the bedridden when they are still physically able, and can exchange their time credits for similar services when they themselves get older and less physically able.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Such social connection helps to fight elderly loneliness and reduces reliance —

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: — on financial resources of the elderly in old age.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Caring for elderly parents is a heavy responsibility that many Singaporeans bear.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And it can take a toll on their physical and mental health, leading to burnout.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many caregivers are women or single adults who sacrifice their careers and/or personal lives to be caregivers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our society must recognise caregivers' challenges and give them more support.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will help more middle-income earners who struggle with the cost of caregiving.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, caregivers sometimes need temporary nursing home places for their loved ones, so that they can occasionally travel or have some respite care.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can MOH expand the availability and accessibility of such temporary nursing home places?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And lastly, I would like to reiterate my call – and that of many other Members – for Family Care Leave to be legislated.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While this is not a panacea to address caregiving challenges, it can be part of a package of help that is extended to caregivers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Implementing these suggestions will go some way to assure caregivers that they have not been forgotten in their difficult and often lonely journey.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, Healthier SG is essential to support ageing in place.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It focuses on preventive care and goes upstream to reduce hospitalisation rates.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To achieve widespread participation and success, there are four critical areas that needs to be addressed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Following these price caps could result in significant earnings loss for them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There is also no guarantee on earnings from Healthier SG payouts, as the number of new patient enrollees and complete cooperation from patients are not guaranteed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Ultimately, managing a private practice is a business venture.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, if GPs believe that joining Healthier SG would result in a loss in earnings, they will hesitate to participate.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In the end, residents lose out because they have fewer GPs to choose from.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In fact, some of them would not even have a choice, because the GP that is nearest or most convenient for them, is not part of the programme.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the MOH address these concerns in time for the rollout in July this year?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, what can seniors expect when Healthier SG is launched?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many seniors have shared with me that they are concerned about what this means for their medical expenses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, there are also some concerns about social prescription, which is a major component of Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some community exercises led by HPB have closed down and have not resumed, even as we resume normalcy post-COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the quantity and variety of Healthier SG activities be increased?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are our healthcare clusters involved in the curation?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can ground-up activities be part of Healthier SG?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If so, can we link them up with ActiveSG, while ensuring that there is no conflict and keeping the overlap of resources minimal?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, with the increasing popularity of home-based medical care services, would these be under Healthier SG?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What are the Ministry's efforts in regulating this sector?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are there steps being taken to ensure the safety and quality of such services for patients who require them?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are there plans to allow the use of MediSave for home care services by approved providers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This could help alleviate the financial burden on patients who require such services and encourage the use of home-based care, where appropriate.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As we promote the shift from hospital to community care, home-based care, too, plays an important role in achieving this and in freeing up hospital resources.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, end-of-life and palliative care should be incorporated into Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should ride on the GP mantra "cradle to grave." Families that have a trusted GP that they have seen for years, will be relieved to continue receiving care with them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As part of this effort, can our GPs promote Advanced Care Planning, or ACP, as part of Healthier SG?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should encourage Singaporeans to tap on the MyLegacy portal for end-of-life planning.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is a good opportunity to involve the wider community, such as lawyers, grassroots, financial planners and religious leaders.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Good palliative care is about providing loving care.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It should be patient-centric care led by nurses and allied healthcare workers, with an empowered family to deliver care, so that seniors can live their lives with dignity and in the care of loved ones in their final days.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: This is especially so, as our people have differing needs and budgets.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: The PAP Senior Group is of the view that we require a whole-of-Government coordination.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: I note that core services to be provided by the AACs, include (a) for active ageing; (b) for befriending; and (c) for referral to care services.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: These are core services that the Silver Generation Office (SGO) and Silver Generation (SG) Ambassadors across the island have been providing for some years now.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Could the Ministry share how it plans for AACs to build on and complement the (a), (b), (c) services that SGO has been providing over the years?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Does the Ministry have plans to scale up our palliative care capabilities and capacities, especially for home-based palliative care, and what might be the challenges?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: I am glad that with this shift, Healthier SG will enable enrolment of Singaporeans, starting with 60 years and above later this year with the emphasis for them to build relationship with a trusted family doctor for their health planning and long-term health management.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: However, we all know that changing behaviours and lifestyle choices which are critical for preventive health and better health outcomes are way harder than popping a pill.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: On this note, I would like to ask what the planning parameters in expansion of AACs.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: I have checked about two years ago for such a centre in a part of my constituency, comprising mostly of 4-room, 5-room, executive and maisonette flats as I often meet seniors who are alone in their flats through my house visits.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: The phenomenon is the same in the private landed housing estates in my constituency.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: Chairman, I have a young cousin who has just entered the nursing profession after graduating from the NAtional University of Singapore (NUS) last year.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: When I asked her what her motivations were to choose the nursing degree, she said that she wanted a job with a purpose, with direct impact to care for people in their most vulnerable times.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: She scored very well in her International Baccalaureate (IB) programme in the School of the Arts Singapore (SOTA) and our family is proud that she opted for the NUS nursing degree without hesitation, even though she had many other degree options.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: She has a sincere heart to care for people.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: However, my heart sinks whenever I read about cases of verbal or even physical abuse towards our nurses and other healthcare workers in our healthcare institutions.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: We owe it to our healthcare workers in bracing through heavy workload in almost three years of fight against the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: On the other hand, I remember the ordeal that my family went through when a loved one was struck by a serious brain virus attack.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: I was promptly asked to go through financial counselling on his admission into the intensive care unit (ICU) to ensure that I am aware of his insurance and eligibility for Government subsidies, before choosing his hospital ward.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: While I gained financial clarity on his hospital stay, my family did not expect the emotional roller coaster in the following three months while his condition went up and down in the hospital.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: We had strong family support to breeze through, some frustrating times when no one had control over his healing.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: But I empathise with some caregivers who are struggling alone, with little support in similar situations and unwittingly turn their anger and frustrations on the nurses and doctors.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is also evidence, both anecdotal and from statistics, that Singapore is losing experienced healthcare practitioners to other countries and to private healthcare.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One of the most often cited reasons is burnout and bad work-life balance.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As Singapore's population ages, the expected number of healthcare professionals needed to meet the rising demand for healthcare is increasing in absolute terms.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thus, this attrition in healthcare staff is clearly not sustainable.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Alternatively, are there active plans to encourage experienced staff that have left the public healthcare system to come back, by making their overall package and working conditions more attractive?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is there a similar committee for nurses and allied healthcare professionals?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There has been a multi-year shortage, and our healthcare workers are overworked.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Looking at the plans for more healthcare facilities and nursing homes coming onstream, we know that many, including Woodlands Health, are struggling with a shortage of nurses and other healthcare manpower, in advance of their opening.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We might say that we are just coming out of a pandemic.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But in truth, the demand for nurses will only get worse as Singapore ages.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There has been welcome news in the past few years of the increase in salaries and efforts to reduce administrative workload.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But recruiting is taking a lot of time and the attrition rates remain high.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Beyond the clinical and non-clinical workload, it is also not uncommon now to hear reports of harassment and abuse from unreasonable patients and families.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Much more needs to be done to educate the public.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Can more be done to entice nurses who have left the profession to rejoin nursing?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Can immigration privileges be temporarily enhanced for trained foreign nurses?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What more game-changing moves is MOH considering, to recruit and retain healthcare workers fast?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, I would like to ask whether the Ministry does any uninformed surveillance across our restructured hospitals of any unfair practice or biases that takes place towards the healthcare workers, for both nurses and even allied health personnel, whose duty is to help clinicians diagnose patients by running necessary tests.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The welfare of healthcare workers and even doctors, starts from management of the hospitals, from the CEO down to line managers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: As fellow Singaporeans, we must never be shy to thank and appreciate them.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We should not condone any forms of abuse towards them and penalise those who cross that line unnecessarily!

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: When I was managing 5,000 bus captains in the past, we had many cases of bus captains being assaulted by passengers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We then worked with the Police, the unions and a few other agencies to create awareness that bus captains are public workers and should not be harassed or assaulted for doing their jobs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In recent years, more and more healthcare workers at public health institutions suffer from harassment or abuse.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Healthcare workers are critical in providing the quality public healthcare that we are enjoying in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Two, is MOH coordinating across all public health institutions to provide a standard protocol to take action against such abusers?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Three, how is MOH working with unions to run campaigns to educate patients and patients' family members to not abuse healthcare workers?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: With joint efforts across different agencies, Mr Chairman, I am confident that healthcare workers can be better protected against harassment, abuse and assault.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As Singapore's population ages, the demand for intermediate and long-term care (ILTC) will continue to increase.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I will focus on manpower in my cut.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Manpower shortages are a key challenge for the ILTC sector.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The ILTC workforce includes doctors, nurses, allied health professionals and social workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: More needs to be done to attract locals to work in the ILTC sector.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: What progress has been made in enhancing salaries, work-life balance, organisational culture, professional development opportunities and fostering a greater sense of purpose towards the profession, particularly in the ILTC sector?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Ministry could also look at attracting non-practicing or retired nurses to return, perhaps on a locum basis, to help relieve the manpower crunch in ILTCs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim also called for this earlier on.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Is MOH looking to encourage more men to enter the profession, so as to boost the overall numbers of nurses?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, our healthcare workers are dedicated individuals who serve industriously on the frontlines.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, despite being mistreated, healthcare workers are obliged to continue looking after their patient, even if it means coming into frequent contact with the abuser, like the patient's caregivers, or even the patients themselves.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is because a healthcare institution cannot endanger a patient's life, by denying service to the patient.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, patients are entitled to medical confidentiality and institutions have policies on media engagement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This may leave healthcare workers unable to respond to false allegations, even when they can be defamatory and lead to the identification and targeting of the employee or their family.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is especially when the abuse is from someone who is not ill, such as a patient's caregiver or relative.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, what if the manner of abuse is egregious or discriminating, such as abuse invoking a person's race or gender?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Do healthcare institutions have policies in place to ensure that these incidents are reported, documented and recorded?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If not, how can we accurately measure the true extent of the problem and take steps to address it?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, when a healthcare worker's reputation is dragged through the mud with false allegations, especially on social media, what is being done to support and protect them?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If the healthcare institution would consider suing for defamation, will patient confidentiality obligations and institutional policies present hurdles for healthcare workers to defend themselves?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are healthcare institutions providing our healthcare workers with adequate support, such as counselling or support groups?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, our healthcare workers play a crucial role in ensuring the delivery of high-quality healthcare services to the population.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, recent reports have highlighted the issue of workplace harassment and abuse faced by healthcare workers, which may harm their mental health and well-being.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We must establish a zero-tolerance policy with clear protocols and say that if you harass or abuse our officers, there will be consequences.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These factors may contribute to shortage of healthcare workers impacting the quality and accessibility of healthcare services.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, I would like to ask the Minister what are the plans to help our healthcare workers grow and to support them, including addressing workplace harassment and abuse, and ensuring the mental health and well-being of healthcare workers are looked after?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time studies have shown that, minimally, 20 teeth are needed to maintain to speak, chew and swallow effectively.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Geriatric dentistry focuses on the oral health of elderly patients, while special care dentistry addresses the unique needs of those with special needs.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: They require specialised knowledge and training to provide the best possible care to these patients.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: What this means is that dentists who decide to specialise in this field do not have a clear route of career progression.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Most would actually need to go through the medical boards of respective institutions and a special appeal process just to get promoted.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: GPs should be able to handle the mild to moderate cases.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, the reality on the ground is that many may not be confident serving such patients and it may incur more costs.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, could MOH consider dentists getting some incentives for the backbreaking work and increased time spent caring for these patients?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: For standard of care, can we have a clinical practice guideline to help ensure quality and appropriate care for these vulnerable populations?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: For example, the United Kingdom (UK) has a clear framework with stratified levels of care for persons with disabilities (PwDs) that we could consider.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Thirdly, Healthier SG is a laudable move in preventive care.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: For dentistry, we have a school dental service that does preventive screening and intervention.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The school dental service covers special education (SPED) schools, but not all, due to limited capacity.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Dental screening uptakes are much lower in SPED schools.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: These children are almost twice as likely to develop caries than those in mainstream schools.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, I hope that in the push for Healthier SG, we do not forget oral healthcare and dentistry, especially for geriatric and special needs patients.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Can MOH tell us more about their plans for these special groups?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: For nurses, how does the Ministry plan to enhance its foreign manpower pipeline, amidst intensifying competition, to complement our local workforce?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: For allied health professionals, does the Ministry plan to increase the capacity of local degree programmes in physiotherapy, radiology, pharmacy and so on?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: For the ILTC sector, how might the Ministry help to ensure that they continue to attract a fair share of healthcare talent?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: For all job groups, how does the Ministry plan to help them practise at the top of their licenses, especially in the community, as part of the Healthier SG strategy?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: I repeat my call to the Ministry to shape more equal roles and more room for co-leadership for healthcare professionals alongside doctors, to prevent and manage chronic diseases across our population.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: I think this requires a mindset shift in our population from a doctor-centric view, to one that equally respects all healthcare professionals, including nurses, allied health professionals and pharmacists.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Leader just told me that I always ask for more and I should ask for less as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As I shared during my Budget speech, many nurses do not get any rest while on shift.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Nurses' dedication to and responsibility for their patients mean that many sacrifice their break time for patients.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should not expect our nurses to work without proper breaks, which places physical, mental and emotional stress on them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can MOH ensure that nurses' breaks during their shifts are protected?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Not only do nurses barely get a chance to rest during their shift, they often get insufficient rest between shifts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is not uncommon for nurses to work overtime and a PM-AM-PM-AM shift – or PAPA shift.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This means that nurses work two consecutive sets of afternoon shifts and morning shifts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many nurses are burnt out and tired and this affects patient safety too.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can MOH look into ensuring that nurses have a minimum amount of rest between shifts, similar to what we do for air stewardesses and air stewards?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, during the height of the pandemic, 900 Singapore Airlines cabin crew were redeployed as Care Ambassadors to support our healthcare staff.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Nurses shared with me that they appreciated the presence of these Care Ambassadors who addressed the patients' service needs, allowing nurses to focus on clinical work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will MOH look into formalising the role of Care Ambassadors and providing our nurses with more support through hiring more ancillary healthcare staff so that they can focus more on clinical work?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Dr Tan Yia Swam, your three cuts, please.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Today, I want to talk about the heart and soul of healthcare.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I am gratified to see many Members of Parliament speaking up for healthcare workers over these recent years and I hope that you will continue to do so, because who heals the healer?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: After three years of fighting COVID-19, healthcare workers are burnt out.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Many feel overworked, underappreciated, even trapped, with no way out.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Many of us entered healthcare because we wanted to help people.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Many were inspired by healthcare workers who attended to our loved ones in their time of need, and we also want to do the same.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: A handful, perhaps, are street smart and see that being a healthcare worker provides a comfortable and steady income.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: But I believe most of us had the calling to serve.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: However, along the way, many of us got jaded.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Some of my doctor and nursing friends have said, they will never allow their children to follow in their footsteps.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: It is too hard – "I don't want them to suffer like I did." People see the glamour of being a doctor.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Maybe they see the top 1%, who are earning very well.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Even here in this House, the perception of the overcharging doctor is prevalent.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, do you know the junior doctor who is the sole income earner looking after his elderly sick parents, a disabled sibling and starts off his career with a large student loan?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Do you know the doctor-nurse couple struggling with infertility because they were too busy, too stressed to try for a family during their training years when they worked shifts and 100-hour work weeks?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Do you know the solo-practice doctor struggling to maintain a viable business, because of increasing manpower and rental costs and falling prey to unfair corporate insurance contracts?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I know there are some really bad doctors out there.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The newspapers, social media are full of these reports.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: But for the rest of us, we have no outlet to share our woes, our struggles.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: We face stressors and problems which the general public is not aware of: Changes in specialist training systems, electronic records which are no better than paper documents placed online.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The use of multiple and, sometimes, duplicate checklists in the name of patient safety.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Increasingly strangulating regulations while complementary health services flourish with no checks or balances – which I will speak more on in my later cut.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Imposition of key performance indicators (KPIs) which drown out what I feel is the most essential – to be a good clinician.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: We lost the ability to listen, to empathise.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: We have short attention spans, are quick to take offence, are quick to judge.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I blame social media, allowing baseless accusations and falsehoods to be amplified by anonymous keyboard warriors.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: When healthcare is managed as a business, healthcare workers become mere service providers, with a fee for service.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Some have self-diagnosed and demand a treatment which they have googled online because they perceive that 20 minutes of Googling is more significant than 20 years of your experience.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: You have all heard about these concerns in October 2020 in the Second Reading of the Medical Registration (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I have spoken on these before and will elaborate on some of these in my later cuts.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: It is this deep sense of unease that is poisoning our entire healthcare ecosystem.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: My gut feel is that we complain about tangible things – asking for more pay, more leave – because we cannot quite express just how sick we feel.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Well, I have just tried, and unless we treat the illness and not just the symptoms, no amount of pay will ever give us back the joy we once had.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Rather than more legislation, I am asking for understanding.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The next time a healthcare worker complains about the system, listen.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The next time a healthcare worker quits and walks away, take the exit interview seriously.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: In the next round of engagements, listen, past the naysayers, to the core issues which are bothering us.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Help us re-establish respect for all healthcare professionals – patient service associates, audiologists, dieticians, medical social workers, lab technicians, podiatrists, couriers – to name but just a few.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Protect us from undue influences by market forces and business entities.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: If you suffer from anxiety or anger management, do not take it out on your healthcare worker; get real help from a mental health professional.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I ask each and every one of you to be understanding, to be kind and help us to help you.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: During my surgical training years in Singapore General Hospital (SGH), I had this highly principled and no-nonsense trainer called Dr Koh Poh Koon – now the Senior Minister of State for Manpower.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I regard him as a man of wisdom and insight, and a mentor to me professionally.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: He said, "GIA's suggestion of using only existing prolonged medical leave insurance or group personal accident insurance in place of WICA would relegate this to a private insurance policy whose terms and conditions are dictated by the insurer without a clear mechanism to adjudicate disputes...

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I do not think we should be leaving it to insurers to be the final arbiter of any disputes to work injury claims," citing possible conflicts of interest.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) is the final arbiter for matters pertaining to the financial viability of insurance companies in Singapore, including IP providers.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: But regrettably, they do not deal with clinical matters.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, it has no teeth and it is not a final arbiter.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: So, who should be the final arbiter for clinical matters in IP policies and claims?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Could there be a law to directly compel IP providers to cover and reimburse healthcare services, in line with acceptable clinical practices or even best practices?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: He had colon cancer, which was operated on several years ago.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: On a follow-up, his oncologist found an abnormal lymph node near the armpit, which he thought was a relapse of the first cancer.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: A core needle biopsy was done to sample the lump and the result was normal.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: However, six months later, that lump grew larger and looked worrying for a different kind of cancer – lymphoma.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Mr B was then referred to me for surgical biopsy.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: This is a surgery to remove the lump for complete testing.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I was a doctor on the patient's insurance panel and completed the pre-authorisation process.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: However, the problem came later on, when even the lab could not make a clear diagnosis and needed to send to another even more specialised lab for a second opinion and additional complex immunohistochemistry (IHC) tests.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The lab needed payment prior to doing the tests and the patient should pay first and reimburse later, but he declined to do so as he had a limited cash flow and was worried that the insurer will not reimburse him, despite written reassurance that he would be.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: In the end, I had to circumvent the issue and asked Mr J, one of the senior managers I know in that insurance company, to help with this.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: On the backend, he personally attended to the case and helped the patient to have cashless payment and got the tests done.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: A few months later, I was asked by the insurance administrator to explain and justify why the second opinion was needed.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: He noted the duplicate request and had it withdrawn.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: But now you know why doctors complain so much about paperwork and insurance.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: This was possible only because of mutual trust.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Mr B trusted his oncologist to recommend the appropriate surgeon for a necessary surgery.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Mr J trusted me – that my medical judgement was sound and my explanations were adequate.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: However, how many patients or doctors enjoy such a relationship with their insurer?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I propose three solutions: (a) insurers can approach a professional body to provide training to their administrators to better process clinical claims; (b) maybe there should be an on-call agent, much like how hospitals have an on-call doctor to attend to any emergency, and this agent will help the clients to navigate the paperwork statim; and (c) perhaps there needs to be a new speciality – a clinical insurer – a medical doctor who changes track mid-career and brings a wealth of clinical knowledge into how insurers should work.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: As our population grows older, more people will be diagnosed with cancers.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: As medical technology advances, there will be newer and better drugs for cancer care, which are costly.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The MOH CDL dictates which drugs will qualify for subsidies and MediSave Coverage.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: IPs providers have also updated their coverage and claim limit terms.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: As a breast surgeon in private practice, most of my patients with breast cancers will be referred to medical oncologists for systemic treatments.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The 2022 median monthly household income was around $10,000.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Using the latest available SingStats Survey on household expenditure ending 2018, I extrapolate: monthly expenditure all in was around $5,800.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: In the report, the monthly housing rental is around $1,000; in current times, monthly rental may range from $2,000 to $3,000.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: So, the surplus may be about $2,000 to $4,000.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: In this family, if someone has cancer and needs treatment, the financial implications are sobering – potential loss of job and loss of income.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: In itself, this is fine, and I have often vouched for the high-quality care in restructured hospitals.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: But it begs the question as to whether the policy intent of IP is met, which is, that insurance will make private services affordable to more people through risk-pooling.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Should there be a big shift of patients to the public sector, it will lead to a further strain on the system, with longer waiting times for appointments and treatments.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Also, do not forget that the subsidies are, ultimately, paid for by taxpayers through the MOH budget.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans should be strongly advised that having an IP does not mean that private healthcare will necessarily be affordable when it comes to cancer care.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: These are difficult issues and we need to think carefully about them.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: This will be a hard lesson for all of us to learn and to accept the practical limits of what we, collectively and individually, can afford.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah
text: In my previous Parliamentary Question in October 2021, it was stated that HDCs may refer patients to NSCs when services capacity or capabilities are not available at the HDCs.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah
text: Where appropriate, HDCs can partner the NSCs to provide an expanded scope of subsidised services at the hospitals based on services, needs and specialty support by the NSCs.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah
text: However, in many of these HDCs, service capacity and capability are already available.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah
text: What commonly happens is that the patients may be able to have a full range of crowns, bridges and gum treatment done in one hospital at a subsidised rate, and suddenly have to hop over to another hospital to get a wisdom tooth surgery done.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah
text: This is not ideal for continuation of care for the patient.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: I know we have finite resources to meet various needs, but I hope that the Ministry could do more to make healthcare affordable for non-Singaporeans with a clear and immediate Singaporean nexus because, ultimately, we are helping their Singaporean loved ones, too.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: Mr Chairman, I declare my interest as a breast surgeon in private practice.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: I work closely with allied health professionals, such as physiotherapists, diagnostic radiographers, radiation therapists and TCM practitioners, whom I know and acknowledge as fellow health professionals.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: I am alarmed by anecdotal reports – some from my patients, some from newspapers – of patients who have suffered unusual complications from some forms of treatment.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: One, free filler injections into the breast, which interferes with screening mammograms for breast cancers permanently.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: Some present years later with pain and infection, requiring surgery.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: These complications cause significant scarring and cosmetic defects in appearance.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: Two, international news reported a few deaths after chiropractor manipulations.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: In a 2018 Channel News Asia (CNA) article, Dr Yap – then-President of the Chiropractic Association – himself asked for regulation, so that patients can make a safer choice.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: Three, people who have received Botox or other invasive beauty treatments in Housing and Developemnt Board (HDB) flats – a few victims have reported to the Health Sciences Authority (HSA) or MOH, with the culprits being charged and reported in local newspapers.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: These are not new issues and have been brought up before.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: I strongly urge MOH to look into these.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: It is better to prevent problems than having to stress an already over-burdened healthcare system.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: Educate the public and encourage victims to lodge Police reports of battery and assault.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: The wellness industry is booming, with many providers in various forms, such as fitness, mindfulness and life coaches, and many more complementary health services.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: Psychologists and counsellors come from a diverse background and are currently not registered under the Allied Health Professions Act.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: While I believe that the majority of these providers are doing good work, I would like to advise MOH to monitor for any reports of a missed diagnosis, for example, someone with a psychiatric disorder not getting the correct diagnosis or treatment, with adverse outcomes.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: I think we write too responsibly and factually, which is boring, without any sensationalism.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: Should we, and are we, able to regulate these SEO articles?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: If not, can MOH work with other Ministries to educate the public on how to choose the right reading materials?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: We must learn from it and prepare for future health crises.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: An educated population is the best defence we can have.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, for more than a decade, the hon Member Christopher de Souza and myself have been asking for a review of gestational limits for abortions in Singapore, as well as the provision of alternatives to the termination of pregnancies.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We can and we should make a move to lower the gestational limit to 22 weeks, as the science informs us.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is a signal for us, as a pro-family society as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Let us do right by unborn children who do not have a choice to choose their chance at life.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Chairman, motherhood is one of, if not the most, noble of aspirations.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: While I thank MOH for the steps it has taken in the right direction with respect to Elective Egg Freezing (EEF), I feel that the ideal destination is still some distance away.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: However, egg quality declines significantly after age 35.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Women who remain excluded from this option in Singapore hold the general view that "lower chance, lower quantity is still better than no chance at all".

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In MOH's response to my Parliamentary Question filed on 9 May 2022, the Minister mentioned that "MOH will continue to monitor medical advances and review the age limit from time to time".

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Chairman, I declare my interest as an eye doctor in private practice.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: In today's medical setting, a patient would often visit multiple healthcare providers, from their GPs, to polyclinics and then to specialist centres.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: From there, some may be referred to therapy centres or to hospitals where, again, there are many centres with different specialist functions for diagnosis, treatment and care.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Hence, the NEHR is a critical platform for many different healthcare professionals to come together to carry out their work in a healthcare setting.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: They can get quick access to health information electronically, to provide better quality and safer care for our patients.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The system would provide complete and up-to-date information about the patient for their healthcare teams to deliver coordinated care.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: NEHR, which collects patients' health records across different healthcare providers and platforms, will enable the authorised healthcare professionals to have a longitudinal view of the patient's medical history, thus allowing multidisciplinary healthcare professionals across Singapore to access a patient's health records to develop a holistic care plan for the patient.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The doctor would know the information of your blood type, of your allergies and the type of medications that you have been prescribed.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: I understand some reasons given were that there was a lot of paperwork for them.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: I believe some doctors have concerns that using NEHR could result in their medical practice being monitored and controlled, while others cite the lack of technical IT support.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Others said that they are very small clinics with just one to two assistants and could not be able to cope with the transition to NEHR.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: What is MOH doing to get all private healthcare clinics to sign up with NEHR and what are the reasons for holding back?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Getting everyone on board is important in aligning the launch of Healthier SG as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Lastly, I would like to ask what digital platform will the Healthier SG initiative be using.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Currently, on our handphone, we have HealthHub; we have Healthy 365.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Will NEHR be another app that we have to download?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Will all these be integrated into a single app?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: But the vision I shared would be a significant jump from this.
